2021_192_9_d_american_cancer_society_art.paragraph: American Cancer Society consumer health article titled “Cell Phone Towers,” last medically reviewed and last revised June 1, 2020, included in the June 15, 2021 board packet as agenda item 9.D. It states that at this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to radiofrequency (RF) waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects, while cautioning that this does not mean the waves are proven absolutely safe. Ground-level RF energy near typical cellular base stations is described as hundreds to thousands of times less than the safe-exposure limits set by the US Federal Communication Commission, and the ACS itself takes no official position on whether RF radiation causes cancer.
2021_192_9_d_american_cancer_society_art.page:
**Source and status**
Article “Cell Phone Towers” from the American Cancer Society, cancer.org, 1.800.227.2345, written by the American Cancer Society medical and editorial content team. Last Medical Review: June 1, 2020. Last Revised: June 1, 2020. Eleven pages including hyperlinks, additional resources and a reference list. Provided in the June 15, 2021 Troy School District board packet as agenda item 9.D.

**Core conclusion**
At this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to RF waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects; this does not mean the waves have been proven absolutely safe, and most expert organizations agree more research is needed, especially on possible long-term effects.

**How towers expose people**
Base stations can be free-standing towers or mounted on existing structures such as trees, water tanks or tall buildings, and are usually from 50 to 200 feet high. RF waves sit in the electromagnetic spectrum between FM radio waves and microwaves and are non-ionizing, so they do not directly damage DNA, unlike x-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet rays. Antenna energy is directed toward the horizon with some downward scatter. At ground level near typical cellular base stations, RF energy is hundreds to thousands of times less than the US Federal Communication Commission (FCC) limits for safe exposure. Roof exposure can exceed ground levels only very close to and directly in front of antennas. Indoors, energy behind an antenna is hundreds to thousands of times lower than in front, and wood or cement block reduces exposure by a factor of about 10.

**What expert agencies say**
The American Cancer Society has no official position or statement on whether RF radiation from cell phones, towers or other sources causes cancer, and looks to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization, and the US National Toxicology Program (NTP), formed from parts of the National Institutes of Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and Food and Drug Administration. Neither IARC nor NTP has classified the cancer-causing potential of RF waves from cell phone towers specifically. The FCC is quoted stating that emissions from cellular and PCS antennas produce ground-level exposures typically thousands of times below safety limits and that there is no reason to believe such towers could constitute a potential health hazard to nearby residents or students. Based on studies published up until 2011, IARC classified RF radiation as “possibly carcinogenic to humans.” The FDA, reviewing studies published between 2008 and 2018, concluded there is insufficient evidence to support a causal association between radiofrequency radiation exposure and tumor formation. The NTP has not included RF radiation in its Report on Carcinogens.

**Studies cited**
A large British study of families of young children with cancer found no link between a mother's exposure to towers during pregnancy and early childhood cancer risk. Researchers in Taiwan found slightly higher overall cancer risk in children living in towns with estimated RF exposure above the study midpoint, a finding less apparent under other exposure categorizations; both studies relied on estimated rather than measured exposure. Large 2018 studies by the NTP and the Ramazzini Institute in Italy found increased risk of malignant schwannomas, uncommon heart tumors, in male rats but not female rats or mice, with the NTP also reporting possible increased risks of brain and adrenal gland tumors; a 2019 review by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) found the studies' limitations did not allow conclusions about RF energy causing cancer.

**5G**
Earlier generation networks used wavelengths below 6 gigahertz (GHz); 5G uses some of that range plus higher frequencies at the lower end of the millimeter wave spectrum, which ranges from 30 GHz to 300 GHz. These remain non-ionizing. Higher frequency waves travel shorter distances and penetrate objects less well, so 5G requires many more small cells mounted on streetlights, utility poles and buildings, typically at much lower power than macro base stations. Very little research has shown that 5G RF waves are any more or less of a concern than other cellular RF wavelengths.
2021_192_9_d_american_cancer_society_art.verbose:
The American Cancer Society article “Cell Phone Towers,” carrying the cancer.org and 1.800.227.2345 banner, was included in the Troy School District Board of Education packet for June 15, 2021 as agenda item 9.D. Its stated dates are Last Medical Review: June 1, 2020 and Last Revised: June 1, 2020, and it is written by the American Cancer Society medical and editorial content team, described as doctors and oncology certified nurses along with journalists, editors and translators. The material is copyrighted, with reprint requests governed by the ACS Content Usage Policy.

Overview. The article opens by noting that widespread cell phone use in recent decades has led to a large increase in the number of cell phone towers, also known as base stations, placed in communities, and that these towers have electronic equipment and antennas that receive and transmit cell phone signals using radiofrequency (RF) waves. Its central conclusion is that at this time there is no strong evidence that exposure to RF waves from cell phone towers causes any noticeable health effects, but that this does not mean the RF waves have been proven absolutely safe, and most expert organizations agree more research is needed, especially regarding possible long-term effects.

How towers expose people to RF waves. Cell phone base stations can be free-standing towers or mounted on existing structures such as trees, water tanks or tall buildings; antennas must be high enough to cover a given area, and base stations are usually from 50 to 200 feet high. Cell phones communicate with nearby towers mainly through RF waves, a form of energy in the electromagnetic spectrum between FM radio waves and microwaves. Like FM radio waves, microwaves, visible light and heat, RF waves are non-ionizing radiation and do not directly damage the DNA inside cells, which is how stronger ionizing radiation such as x-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet (UV) rays is thought to cause cancer. An electromagnetic spectrum illustration credited to the National Cancer Institute shows frequencies from extremely low (such as power lines) to extremely high (such as x-rays and gamma rays). At very high levels RF waves can heat body tissues, but the levels used by cell phones and towers are much lower. When a call is placed, a signal goes from the phone's antenna to the nearest base station antenna, the base station assigns an available RF channel, RF waves transfer voice information to the base station, and voice signals are sent to a switching center that transfers the call to its destination, with signals relayed back and forth during the call; the RF waves produced at the base station are given off into the environment where people can be exposed.

Exposure by location. On the ground near a tower, RF waves from the antenna are directed toward the horizon, parallel to the ground, with some downward scatter. Base station antennas use higher power levels than other land-mobile antennas but much lower levels than radio and television broadcast stations, and RF energy decreases rapidly as distance from the antenna increases, so ground-level exposure is much lower than exposure close to the antenna. At ground level near typical cellular base stations, the amount of energy from RF waves is hundreds to thousands of times less than the limits for safe exposure set by the US Federal Communication Commission (FCC) and other regulatory authorities, and it is very unlikely a person could be exposed above these limits merely by being near a tower. On a roof with a cellular antenna, a person could be exposed to levels greater than those on the ground, but levels approaching or exceeding FCC safety guidelines are only likely very close to and directly in front of antennas, and access to such areas should be limited. Indoors with a base station mounted on the outside of a building, RF energy is typically much lower than outside, depending on construction materials; antennas point away from the building side, energy behind the antenna is hundreds to thousands of times lower than in front, and wood or cement block reduces exposure by a factor of about 10, so exposure in a room directly behind the wall is typically well below recommended exposure limits.

What expert agencies say. The American Cancer Society (ACS) does not have any official position or statement on whether RF radiation from cell phones, cell phone towers or other sources causes cancer, and generally looks to other expert organizations to determine whether something is a carcinogen, including the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization (WHO), and the US National Toxicology Program (NTP), formed from parts of several government agencies including the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). So far neither IARC nor the NTP has classified the cancer-causing potential of RF waves from cell phone towers specifically. The article quotes the FCC on towers near homes or schools: radiofrequency emissions from antennas used for cellular and PCS (personal communications service) transmissions result in exposure levels on the ground that are typically thousands of times below safety limits, limits adopted by the FCC based on recommendations of expert organizations and endorsed by federal agencies responsible for health and safety, so there is no reason to believe such towers could constitute a potential health hazard to nearby residents or students.

On RF radiation generally, IARC, based on a review of studies published up until 2011, classified RF radiation as “possibly carcinogenic to humans,” citing limited evidence of a possible increase in risk for brain tumors among cell phone users and inadequate evidence for other cancer types. More recently the US FDA issued a technical report based on studies published between 2008 and 2018 as well as national cancer rate trends, concluding there is insufficient evidence to support a causal association between radiofrequency radiation (RFR) exposure and tumor formation. The NTP has not included RF radiation in its Report on Carcinogens, which lists exposures known to be or reasonably anticipated to be human carcinogens.

Studies described. Researchers generally use studies looking at groups of people and studies done in the lab using lab animals or cell cultures. Few studies in people have focused specifically on cellular phone towers and cancer risk, and results have not provided clear answers. A large British study comparing families of young children with cancer to families of children without cancer found no link between a mother's exposure to towers during pregnancy, based on distance from home to the nearest tower and on RF energy given off by nearby towers, and the risk of early childhood cancer. Researchers in Taiwan comparing children with cancer to similar children without cancer found slightly higher overall cancer risk among those living in towns with estimated RF exposure from towers above the study's midpoint level, though the finding was less apparent when exposure was categorized in other ways. Both studies relied on estimated rather than measured RF exposure. Exposure from living near a tower is typically many times lower than exposure from using a cell phone; several dozen studies have examined links between cell phone use and tumors, and most have not found a link, with important limitations noted.

Lab studies. RF waves from towers do not have enough energy to damage DNA directly or heat body tissues, so it is not clear how towers might cause cancer. Large studies published in 2018 by the US National Toxicology Program and by the Ramazzini Institute in Italy exposed groups of lab rats, and mice in the NTP study, to whole-body RF waves for many hours a day beginning before birth and continuing for most or all of their natural lives. Both found an increased risk of uncommon heart tumors called malignant schwannomas in male rats but not in female rats, nor in male or female mice in the NTP study; the NTP study also reported possible increased risks of certain brain and adrenal gland tumors. A 2019 review of the two studies by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP) determined that their limitations did not allow conclusions about the ability of RF energy to cause cancer, though the results do not rule out the possibility of health impacts.

5G networks. Fifth generation cellular networks are being rolled out in the United States and other countries and can transmit much larger amounts of data over shorter periods than 4G, 3G and earlier generations. Earlier generations used RF wavelengths below 6 gigahertz (GHz); 5G uses some wavelengths in that range plus higher frequencies at the lower end of the millimeter wave spectrum, which ranges from 30 GHz to 300 GHz. These higher-frequency waves remain non-ionizing and still lack the ability to directly damage DNA. Because they travel shorter distances and pass less well through objects such as buildings or tree leaves, 5G requires many more small cells, which can be mounted on streetlights, utility poles, buildings and other structures, placing antennas closer to people while typically operating at much lower power than larger macro base stations. Adding higher wavelengths could expose people to more RF waves overall, though higher frequency waves penetrate the body less and in theory might be less likely to have health effects; this has not been well studied, and there has been very little research showing 5G RF waves are any more or less of a concern than other cellular RF wavelengths.

Resources and references. Additional resources listed include the FCC RF Safety FAQ, the FDA Cell Phones page, the National Cancer Institute fact sheets on Cell Phones and Cancer Risk and Electromagnetic Fields and Cancer, and National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences pages on Electric and Magnetic Fields and Cell Phone Radio Frequency Radiation, with a note that inclusion does not imply ACS endorsement. Cited references include ANSI-C95.1, 1982, American National Standards Institute, safety levels for human exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, 300 kHz to 100 GHz; Elliott P, Toledano MB, Bennett J, et al., Mobile phone base stations and early childhood cancers: Case-control study, BMJ 2010;340:c3077; Falcioni L, Bua L, Tibaldi E, et al., report on brain and heart tumors in Sprague-Dawley rats exposed from prenatal life until natural death to a mobile phone radiofrequency field representative of a 1.8GHz GSM base station environmental emission, Environ Res 2018;165:496-503; FCC Office of Engineering and Technology RF Safety FAQ, 2015, accessed December 30, 2019; FDA, Review of Published Literature between 2008 and 2018 of Relevance to Radiofrequency Radiation and Cancer, 2020, accessed March 19, 2020;
